newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN says Burma will join but dodges timing.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN says Burma will join but dodges timing.

text.p: Heads of government of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) decided at a summit on Saturday to admit Burma as a full member despite Western pressure, but stopped short of saying when.
Foreign Minister Ali Alatas of host nation Indonesia said the summit decided to admit all three observer nations Burma, Laos and Cambodia into the group simultaneously but had not set a time.
ASEAN currently has seven members -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
"There is no difference whatsoever among the members of ASEAN as to the principle of Burma's entry into ASEAN," Alatas told reporters.

"Whatever nuances of differences there were in the past was on the timing. At this meeeting it is agreed by all heads of state that all three (observers) will enter together. As to the timing of the entry, that will be announced in due time."
Diplomats have said Laos and Cambodia are on track to join ASEAN at its 30th anniversary celebrations in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur in July next year.
Alatas said no precise time had been set, but added: "You can draw your own conclusions."

Western nations and human rights activists have put pressure on ASEAN to at least delay the admission of Burma, citing the Rangoon military government's crackdown on the pro-democracy movement led by Nobel peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
ASEAN has maintained that it will not respond to external pressure on the issue and has said isolating Rangoon may be counter-productive.

But some ASEAN leaders, including Philippine President Fidel Ramos and Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, have said in the past month that Burma may not yet be ready to join, throwing up differences in the normally united group.
Diplomats have said Malaysia and Indonesia are in favour of quickly admitting Burma.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad told reporters after the summit that ASEAN's policy of constructive engagement, or maintaining links, with Burma had led to some reform there.
"If anybody says constructive engagement has not had a constructive effect, they must be thoroughly blind," he said.
Burmese Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw said Rangoon accepted the decision.
Asked at a news conference if he was disappointed that no timetable had been set, he said: "We do not have any comment over that. We not insist upon what time we should be integrated."
But he later added: "There is no reason why we should not be happy."

ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh said Burma was on track to complete technical requirements to join the ASEAN Free Trade Area, including a programme to reduce tariffs and non-tariff trade barriers and meet investment requirements.
He said of the technical process which Burma has to undergo before full membership: "Our speed is comfortable for everybody. If it is uncomfortable, we should not bring them in."
